title: Anyone Used AI Scaffolding?
author: KedericTheOgre
selftext:
I’ve seen some great results setting up AI Scaffolding around my game dev process. 

I’m just feeling this out and not formally trained, but hear me out:

At first I was just iterating, but once I exhausted a context window and the codebase grew beyond say 100k lines, I was frustrated with the mutations and unintended changes.

I took some time to set up what I call an AI Scaffold, but it was worth it.

I set up five layers:

Game Constitution: what I am building (yaml)  
|  
AI Operating System: how agents should build (yaml)  
|  
Unified Registry: what is built so far (md)  
|  
Game Engine, Event Bus, UI: the game itself  
|  
Digital Twin: An AI friendly rendition of the game

Every time I set an agent loose on the game, I have them review the scaffold layer by layer. They know what my creative vision is, what their boundaries are, gap fit what I want vs what is built, they they build a slice, see the result, and update the registry with what they did. Then repeat.

I have found I get faster results, lower token usage, and greater comfort in letting an agent iterate for 24-48 hours with minimal supervision.

Anyone else have frameworks they have used to guide agents effectively?

comments.author: Ferniclestix
comments.body:
my codebase is quite large on both my main projects.

I use a modular framework so that each function and component gets split into function based files.  
I build template kits for regularly used functions like a text entry box for example. instead of re-writing it 20 times across the project it always refers back to that one kit to do the job.

I periodically do an 'audit' where we go over the project and pull things out if they dont fit in a particular function file.

I also have a project directory, changelog and 'ai notes' which is specifically a file for the AI to give itself notes.

The project directory has a system architecture section to describe what each function and system does including class listing and other documentation.

my setup is designed to allow a random AI with directory control to step in and pick things up with no context or knowledge about the project and be able to get to work.  
because it also works on small files  its hallucinations are limited in scope and usually just amount to duplicated function and not puitting things in the right place  rather than losing or breaking existing features.

https://i.redd.it/x4ud80h98b1i1.png

the pic is a look at my current project directory.

  
tho im hands on with my AI crreation, i dont just let it go ham :)

comments.author: CromagnonV
comments.body: I just use boring old SDLC practices like architecture documentation, product requirements, build specs and test cases. With at least 1 agent at each level enforcing their domain.

comments.author: JakSilver00
comments.body:
I mean I kind of have something similar to that, but it's not limited to game development. I wouldn't necessarily call it a scaffolding since it's across all my files and I don't exclusively work on game development, but it's basically like an index, instructions, rolling handoffs, project type-based instructions and skills.  
But yeah, it significantly improved the performance and efficiency of it. Additionally, if you use Python or something like n8n to run all the repetitive deterministic automations, That the agents can build when they need them. you can be doing max level things on a pro subscription.
